q: Loop 10 has five project options. The single most-important rule for picking is: pick the smaller one. Why does this rule beat 'pick the most ambitious one your skills can handle'?
answer_outline: Capstones that ship beat capstones that don't, every time. An ambitious project that takes 60 hours and gets abandoned at hour 35 produces nothing — no demo, no README, no postmortem. A modest project that takes 25 hours and ships at hour 25 produces a complete artifact: a deployed instance you can show, a README that documents trade-offs, a postmortem that captures lessons. The 'lessons' from a abandoned ambitious capstone are mostly bitterness; the lessons from a finished modest capstone are durable knowledge about scope, cost, and shipping. Builder-first is graded on shipping. Pick the option that's safely inside your timeline, then *use the time saved* to improve quality on what you built rather than to add features.

q: Why is the postmortem 'non-negotiable' — what specifically does it produce that the rest of the capstone deliverables don't?
answer_outline: Three things only the postmortem produces. (1) Honest delta between plan and reality. SPEC.md is the plan; the deployed agent is the result; only the postmortem documents *what changed and why*. Without it, future-you can't tell which decisions were good calls and which were costly. (2) Surface area for the lessons. Code captures *what was built*; the postmortem captures *what was almost built and shouldn't have been*. The 'over-engineered' section is often where the most expensive lesson lives. (3) Forward transferability. Six weeks from now, you'll start another agent project and forget specifically why you cut chat history in week 1, or why you went plain Python over LangGraph, or what your retry policy actually did. The postmortem is a letter to that future-you. Lessons not written down do not transfer; the rest of the capstone produces working code, but only the postmortem produces *durable judgment*.

q: After Loop 10, which curriculum-spanning patterns should you be able to recognize *without* looking up which loop they came from?
answer_outline: Roughly: (Loop 1) the agent loop is just a while-loop wrapping LLM calls; the model is stateless and you carry history. (Loop 2) tool use needs structured output channels and descriptive error contracts. (Loop 3) ReAct is a pattern for reasoning, and traces are how you debug agents. (Loop 4) agent state is just files and dicts — memory, context, and tools are all manipulable objects. (Loops 5/6) frameworks abstract conventions; LangChain saves boilerplate, LangGraph adds branching/visibility, both pin specific versions and churn fast. (Loop 7a) architecture isn't free; benchmark before claiming it helps. (Loop 7b) most multi-agent designs are role-play in costume; the test is 'is this just one agent with bad prompts'. (Loop 8) hybrid retrieval beats sparse or dense alone, but RAG isn't always the right answer. (Loop 9) production agents are graded on numbers — caching, retries, cost, observability, deploy — and most of them are orthogonal to agent quality. (Loop 10) shipping requires scope cut and postmortems to convert experience into durable judgment. If you can recite this list with one or two sentences each from memory, you've internalized builder-first.
